citation.title: On the Foundations of the Design-Based Approach

standing_assumptions:
The work is a main article of 16 pages (Political Analysis (2026), 0, 1–16, doi:10.1017/pan.2026.10045; printed page = PDF page) and a publisher's Supplementary Appendix of 10 pages (publisher-supplement.pdf; printed page = PDF page, the first page unnumbered). The main text states no numbered theorem: its formal content is the setup of Section 3, Equations (1)–(8), Conditions 4.1, 5.1 and 5.2 and the worked Tables 1–5. The supplement carries its own Equations (1)–(11), Conditions 1.1–1.3 and Proposition 1; they are cited below as ‘supplement Equation (k)’ and so on. Everything quoted was read from the page images.
(S1) Probability space. p. 3, Section 3: “we formalize the design in terms of a probability triple $(\Omega,S,P)$, where the sample space, $\Omega$, consists of all conceivable experimental (or sampling) interventions and each realized intervention, $\omega$, refers to the vector of treatment (or sampling) assignments to all $N$ observations. The event space is the power set of the sample space, $S=\mathcal P(\Omega)$ and we assume that our probability measure satisfies $\Pr[A]=\sum_{\omega\in A}p(\omega),\ \forall A\in S$, where $p:\Omega\to[0,1]$, with $p(\omega)$ characterizing the probability of the assignment of an intervention.”
(S2) Design and design space. p. 3, Section 3.1: “We define the design space $\mathcal Z=\mathbf Z(\Omega)$, where $\mathbf Z$ is a bijective random vector $\mathbf Z:\Omega\to\mathbb R^N$. The design is defined as the joint p.m.f. of $\mathbf Z$, $f:\mathbb R^N\to[0,1]$. We may define all objects with respect to the design vector $\mathbf Z$, removing all notational dependence on $\omega$. We assume that the design is determined by the researcher”. ‘Bijective’ is read as injective, that is, a bijection of $\Omega$ onto $\mathcal Z$ (finding P061-N003, a clarity note); the inverse in Equation (1) is applied only on $\mathcal Z$. $\mathcal Z$ is the set of feasible interventions and may be strictly larger than the support of the design (p. 8: “$\mathcal Z$ may include assignments outside the design”).
(S3) Population and raw potential outcomes. p. 4, Section 3.2: “This finite population is indexed by $i=1,\ldots,N$, where indexing is fixed.” “We represent the outcomes of interest associated with these units with a real-valued random vector, $\mathbf Y$. The random vector $\mathbf Y$ characterizes the raw potential outcomes, which can be represented for each individual $i$ as $$y_i(\mathbf z)=Y_i(\mathbf Z^{-1}(\mathbf z)),\ \forall i\in 1,\ldots,N,\ \mathbf z\in\mathcal Z.\qquad(1)$$ The raw potential outcome $y_i(\mathbf z)$ for individual $i$ is what we observe if we perform intervention $\mathbf z$ and measure unit $i$’s outcome. There are a total of $N\times|\mathcal Z|$ raw potential outcomes in the causal setting.” The observed outcome is $Y_i=y_i(\mathbf Z)$ (supplement p. 2: “we use the fact that $Y_i=y_i(\mathbf Z)$, from the definition of raw potential outcomes given in Section 3”).
(S4) Exposure mapping. p. 4, Section 3.3: “Formally, our exposure mapping for individual $i$ is a function $g_i:\mathcal Z\to\mathbb R$.” “Given that we have knowledge of the support of the design vector, $\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)$, we can define a function $g_i|_{\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)}:\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)\to\mathbb R$. We denote the $N$-length random exposure vector $$\mathbf D=(g_1(\mathbf Z),g_2(\mathbf Z),\ldots,g_N(\mathbf Z)).\qquad(2)$$” The mappings used in the paper's examples: the ‘individualistic’ mapping (p. 5) $g_i(\mathbf z)=\begin{cases}1&:z_i=1\\0&:\text{otherwise}\end{cases},\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N$ (written $g_i(\mathbf z)=z_i$ on p. 8); the network mapping (p. 5) $$g_i(\mathbf z)=\begin{cases}0\ (\text{Control})&:\text{ if }z_i=0\text{ and }\theta_i\mathbf z=0,\\1\ (\text{Isolated Direct})&:\text{ if }z_i=1\text{ and }\theta_i\mathbf z=0,\\2\ (\text{Indirect})&:\text{ if }z_i=0\text{ and }\theta_i\mathbf z>0,\\3\ (\text{Direct \& Indirect})&:\text{ if }z_i=1\text{ and }\theta_i\mathbf z>0,\end{cases}\quad\forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\ \mathbf z\in\{0,1\}^N,\qquad(3)$$ “where $\theta_i$ is the $i$th row of the network adjacency matrix”; and the coarsened mapping of Section 6.2 (p. 11) $g_i(\mathbf z)=\begin{cases}1&:z_i>0\\0&:\text{otherwise}\end{cases},\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\},\mathbf z\in\{0,1,2\}^N$.
(S5) Exposure probability, positivity, EPO. p. 6, Section 4.1: “we denote the marginal probability that unit $i$ enters exposure $d$ under the design distribution of $\mathbf Z$ as $$\pi_i(d)=\Big(\sum_{\mathbf z\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z):g_i(\mathbf z)=d}\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]\Big)=\Pr[D_i=d].\qquad(4)$$” “Condition 4.1 (Individual positivity). An exposure $d$ satisfies individual positivity if there exists a $c$ such that $0<c\le\pi_i(d)\ \forall i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$.” “Given that relevant individual positivity assumptions hold, the EPO for unit $i$ under exposure $d$ is defined as $$\overline y_i(d)=\frac{\sum_{\mathbf z\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z):g_i(\mathbf z)=d}y_i(\mathbf z)\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]}{\sum_{\mathbf z\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z):g_i(\mathbf z)=d}\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]}=\mathrm E[y_i(\mathbf Z)|g_i(\mathbf Z)=d]=\mathrm E[y_i(\mathbf Z)|D_i=d].\qquad(5)$$” “To avoid notational overload, these definitions implicitly hold fixed the exposure mapping $g$ and design $\mathbf Z$.” Where two designs are compared the paper writes $\tau_{\mathbf Z}$, $\tau_{\mathbf Z'}$ (Tables 4 and 5, Section 6.3).
(S6) AEPO, EED, AEED. p. 7: “Under individual positivity (Condition 4.1) for exposure $d$ and all individuals $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$, we average the EPOs over the units in the population to define the AEPO as $$\overline y(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\overline y_i(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[y_i(\mathbf Z)|D_i=d].\qquad(6)$$” “For an individual observation $i$, assuming that Condition 4.1 holds for exposures $d$ and $d'$ for all individuals $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$, we can define the EED between $d$ and $d'$ as $$\tau_i(d,d')=\overline y_i(d)-\overline y_i(d').\qquad(7)$$” “The AEED between $d$ and $d'$ is $$\tau(d,d')=\overline y(d)-\overline y(d')=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\tau_i(d,d').\qquad(8)$$” Footnote 8 (p. 7): “We compare this to the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect defined in Sävje, Aronow, and Hudgens (2021): $\tau_i^{AC}(d,d',\mathbf z_{-i})=y_i(d;\mathbf z_{-i})-y_i(d';\mathbf z_{-i})$. In the assignment-conditional unit-level treatment effect, we hold constant treatments assigned to all other individuals at $\mathbf z_{-i}$.”
(S7) Stability conditions. p. 8, Section 5.1: “Condition 5.1 (NURVA). $$g_i(\mathbf z)=g_i(\mathbf z')\implies y_i(\mathbf z)=y_i(\mathbf z')=\overline y_i(g_i(\mathbf z)),\ \forall\mathbf z,\mathbf z'\in\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z).$$” “Condition 5.2 (SUTVA). $$g_i(\mathbf z)=g_i(\mathbf z')\implies y_i(\mathbf z)=y_i(\mathbf z')=\overline y_i(g_i(\mathbf z)),\ \forall\mathbf z,\mathbf z'\in\mathcal Z.$$”
(S8) Estimator. Supplement p. 1: “Throughout, we will require the individual positivity, Condition 4.1, referenced in Section 4.” “We use the Horvitz-Thompson inverse probability weighted estimator (Horvitz and Thompson 1952), as defined in Equation 1, $$\hat{\overline y}(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Y_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}.\qquad(1)$$” Supplement p. 4: “For the AEED, define $\hat\tau(d,d')=\hat{\overline y}(d)-\hat{\overline y}(d')$ and $\pi_{ij}(d,d')=\Pr[D_i=d,D_j=d']$.” Supplement p. 3: “Let the joint exposure probability, $\pi_{ij}(d)=\Pr[D_i=D_j=d]$.”
(S9) Asymptotic regime. Supplement p. 5: “We define a sequence of finite populations $U_{(N)}$ indexed by population size $N$. Associated with each finite population $U_{(N)}$ is a known random design vector $\mathbf Z_{(N)}$, a feasible intervention set $\mathcal Z_{(N)}$, $N$ exposure mappings $g_{i,(N)}:\mathcal Z_{(N)}\to\mathbb R$, and $N\times|\mathcal Z_{(N)}|$ raw potential outcomes. Assume that the range of $g_{i,(N)}|\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z_{(N)})$ contains $d$, for all $i,N$. The observed data is $(\mathbf Z_{(N)},\mathbf Y_{(N)})$. We let $N$ tend to infinity.” Note 2 (supplement p. 10): “In the asymptotic regime we could also index observations of, e.g., $y_i$ and $\pi_i(d)$ by $(N)$ but we leave this indexing implicit below.”
(S10) What the paper does not state, and how it is read here. (a) $\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z)$ is not defined; it is read as $\{\mathbf z\in\mathcal Z:\Pr[\mathbf Z=\mathbf z]>0\}$. (b) ‘Finite population’ restricts $N$, not the number of assignments: by (S1) the support is countable, and nothing makes it finite. Every design in the paper's examples and tables has finite support; the general setup admits a countably infinite support with unbounded outcomes (finding P061-CAND-001). (c) No integrability condition is stated anywhere. (d) Conditions 5.1 and 5.2 print no quantifier over $i$; they are read as holding for every $i\in\{1,\ldots,N\}$. Their last equality, $=\overline y_i(g_i(\mathbf z))$, involves an EPO that Equation (5) defines only when $\pi_i(g_i(\mathbf z))>0$: under Condition 5.1 this is automatic and the equality follows from the first one; under Condition 5.2 it is read as holding wherever the EPO is defined (finding P061-CAND-003, a clarity note, whose repair deletes that equality from Condition 5.2). (e) The notation $y_i(d;\mathbf z_{-i})$ of footnote 8 is not defined further; it is read as the raw potential outcome at the assignment vector whose $i$th coordinate is $d$ and whose other coordinates are $\mathbf z_{-i}$, which presupposes that the labels $d,d'$ are assignment coordinates and that the hybrid vector lies in $\mathcal Z$. (f) All probabilities, expectations, variances and covariances are over the design distribution of $\mathbf Z$, with the raw potential outcomes fixed.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplementary Appendix, Equation (2) and the ‘key take-away’ after Equation (3): reduction to the sample mean and the difference in means, unbiased without NURVA
canonical_claim.location: Supplementary Appendix p. 1 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 1) for Equation (2); p. 2 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 2) for the take-away sentence
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed (supplement p. 1): ‘Suppose that exposure is individualistic, and we have a simple random sampling strategy of $n$ of $N$ units into exposure $d$. Then the Horvitz-Thompson estimator is equivalent to the sample mean, as shown in Equation 2: $$\hat{\overline y}(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Y_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Y_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{n/N}=\frac{N}{nN}\sum_{i=1}^NY_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^NY_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}=\frac1n\sum_{i:D_i=d}Y_i.\qquad(2)$$’ (supplement p. 2): ‘A key take-away from the unbiasedness of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator is that even without NURVA, in standard (simple random sampling without replacement) surveys, the sample mean is unbiased for the AEPO and in standard (completely randomized) experiments the difference-in-means estimator is unbiased for the AEED.’
Formal content. (a) If $\pi_i(d)=n/N$ for every $i$, then $\hat{\overline y}(d)=\frac1n\sum_{i:D_i=d}Y_i$; when exactly $n$ units are in exposure $d$ on every assignment in the support, this is the sample mean of the outcomes of the units in exposure $d$. (b) Survey: if the set of units in exposure $d$ (‘sampled’) is a simple random sample of $n$ of the $N$ units, without replacement, then $\mathrm E\big[\frac1n\sum_{i:D_i=d}Y_i\big]=\overline y(d)$, whatever the raw potential outcomes $y_i(\mathbf z)$ (no NURVA). (c) Experiment: if $\mathcal Z\supseteq\{0,1\}^N$, $g_i(\mathbf z)=z_i$ and $\mathbf Z$ is uniform on the assignments in $\{0,1\}^N$ with exactly $n_1$ ones ($1\le n_1\le N-1$), then $$\mathrm E\Big[\frac1{n_1}\sum_{i:Z_i=1}Y_i-\frac1{N-n_1}\sum_{i:Z_i=0}Y_i\Big]=\tau(1,0),$$ whatever the raw potential outcomes (no NURVA).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat{\overline y}(d)$: supplement Equation (1), p. 1 (S8). ‘Individualistic’ exposure: p. 5, the mapping that codes a unit by its own assignment (S4). A simple random sampling strategy of $n$ of $N$ units into exposure $d$: the set $\{i:D_i=d\}$ is uniformly distributed over the subsets of size $n$, so $\pi_i(d)=n/N$; the paper's own survey example (p. 3) records the order of sampling in $\mathbf Z$ and uses $g_i(\mathbf z)=\mathbb 1\{z_i>0\}$ (p. 4), for which the set of surveyed groups is a simple random sample of 3 of 10 and $\pi_i(1)=3/10$. A completely randomized experiment: exactly $n_1$ of the $N$ units are assigned to treatment, all such assignments being equally likely; the symbol $n_1$ is not the paper's. AEPO and AEED: Equations (6) and (8), p. 7 (S6). Unbiasedness of $\hat{\overline y}(d)$: supplement Equation (3) (P061-T16).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P061-H5, second part; both readers confirmed the reduction, and the Opus reader confirmed by enumeration that under complete randomization the difference in means has expectation equal to the AEED ($\tfrac{3}{10}$ in its example) with NURVA violated. The chain of Equation (2) uses only $\pi_i(d)=n/N$; the hypothesis ‘individualistic’ is not used in the algebra. The take-away sentence is prose: (b) and (c) are its formal content, obtained from (a) and supplement Equation (3); the definitions of the two ‘standard’ designs are the conventional ones and are fixed above. Since these designs have finite support, finding P061-CAND-001 does not touch this target.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplementary Appendix, Equations (4), (5) and (9): the estimator and its exact variance under NURVA, and the variance of the AEED estimator
canonical_claim.location: Supplementary Appendix p. 2 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 2) for Equation (4); p. 3 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 3) for Equation (5); p. 4 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 4) for Equation (9)
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. Supplement p. 2: ‘Under NURVA, we remove all implicit probabilistic dependence of $Y_i$ on $\mathbf Z$: $$\hat{\overline y}(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Y_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{\overline y_i(d)\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\Pr[D_i=d]}.\qquad(4)$$’ Supplement p. 3: ‘Let the joint exposure probability, $\pi_{ij}(d)=\Pr[D_i=D_j=d]$. Then under NURVA, the variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator is $$\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]=N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\mathrm{Cov}[\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\},\mathbb 1\{D_j=d\}]\frac{\overline y_i(d)\overline y_j(d)}{\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}=N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{\pi_{ij}(d)-\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}{\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}\overline y_i(d)\overline y_j(d).\qquad(5)$$’ Supplement p. 4: ‘For the AEED, define $\hat\tau(d,d')=\hat{\overline y}(d)-\hat{\overline y}(d')$ and $\pi_{ij}(d,d')=\Pr[D_i=d,D_j=d']$. Under NURVA, $$\mathrm{Var}\{\hat\tau(d,d')\}=\mathrm{Var}\{\hat{\overline y}(d)\}+\mathrm{Var}\{\hat{\overline y}(d')\}-2\mathrm{Cov}\{\hat{\overline y}(d),\hat{\overline y}(d')\},$$ $$\mathrm{Cov}\{\hat{\overline y}(d),\hat{\overline y}(d')\}=N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{\pi_{ij}(d,d')-\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d')}{\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d')}\overline y_i(d)\overline y_j(d').\qquad(9)$$’
Hypotheses: the setting of Section 3; Condition 4.1 for $d$ (for $d$ and $d'$ in Equation (9)); Condition 5.1 (NURVA).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat{\overline y}(d)$: supplement Equation (1), p. 1 (S8). $\overline y_i(d)$: Equation (5) of the main text, p. 6 (S5). Condition 5.1: p. 8 (S7), read as in (S10)(d). $\pi_{ij}(d)=\Pr[D_i=D_j=d]$ (so $\pi_{ii}(d)=\pi_i(d)$) and $\pi_{ij}(d,d')=\Pr[D_i=d,D_j=d']$ (so $\pi_{ii}(d,d')=0$ when $d\ne d'$, as the supplement notes on p. 4). Variances and covariances are over the design distribution. The identity behind Equation (4): under NURVA, $Y_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}=\overline y_i(d)\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}$ on the support.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P061-H6, the exact variance expression; both readers derived Equations (4), (5) and (9) by hand and confirmed them by exact enumeration (Equation (5) exact in each of 220 design and exposure cases). The sentence introducing Equation (4) is the clarity note P061-APP-002 (NURVA removes within-exposure variation on the support, not ‘all’ dependence of $Y_i$ on $\mathbf Z$); Equation (4) itself is correct. The supplement adds that without NURVA Equation (5) ‘no longer gives the variance in terms of fixed exposure-level potential outcomes’; that caveat is not part of this target. No error-class finding touches it; on designs with infinite support NURVA already supplies the first moments (P061-T8(iv)), and second moments are finite for the same reason.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplementary Appendix, Equations (6), (7) and (8): the unbiased Horvitz–Thompson variance estimator when all joint exposure probabilities are positive, and the conservative variance estimator under NURVA
canonical_claim.location: Supplementary Appendix p. 3 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 3) for Equation (6); p. 4 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 4) for Equations (7) and (8)
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. Supplement p. 3: ‘When NURVA does hold, first, suppose for illustrative purposes that $\pi_{ij}(d)>0$ for all $i,j$. Then we could obtain the Horvitz-Thompson estimator of the variance of the Horvitz-Thompson estimator, and it is straightforwardly unbiased. This estimated variance is, $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HT}}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]=N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{\pi_{ij}(d)-\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}{\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}Y_iY_j\frac{\mathbb 1\{D_i=D_j=d\}}{\pi_{ij}(d)},\qquad(6)$$ with $\mathrm E[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HT}}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]]=N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N\frac{\pi_{ij}(d)-\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}{\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}\overline y_i(d)\overline y_j(d)$ by linearity of expectations. Now, suppose that $\pi_{ij}(d)=0$ for some $i,j$. The issue is that there is no longer an unbiased estimator for $\overline y_i(d)\overline y_j(d)$ since this product is never observed. However, a quick upper bound is available from Young’s inequality: $|\overline y_i(d)\overline y_j(d)|\le\frac{\overline y_i(d)^2}{2}+\frac{\overline y_j(d)^2}{2}$’. Supplement pp. 3–4: ‘This bound admits an unbiased estimator that depends only on marginal exposure probabilities. Thus Equation 7 provides a “conservative” variance estimator: $$\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm C}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]=N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j:\pi_{ij}(d)>0}\frac{\pi_{ij}(d)-\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}{\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)}Y_iY_j\frac{\mathbb 1\{D_i=D_j=d\}}{\pi_{ij}(d)}+N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j:\pi_{ij}(d)=0}\Big(\frac{Y_i^2}{2}\frac{\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}+\frac{Y_j^2}{2}\frac{\mathbb 1\{D_j=d\}}{\pi_j(d)}\Big).\qquad(7)$$ This gives us the desired result that under NURVA, the Horvitz-Thompson variance estimator is conservative, $$\mathrm E[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm C}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]]\ge\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\overline y}(d)].\qquad(8)$$’
Formal content. In the setting of Section 3, under Condition 4.1 for $d$ and Condition 5.1: (a) if $\pi_{ij}(d)>0$ for all $i,j$, then $\mathrm E[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm{HT}}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]]=\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]$; (b) with no condition on the joint exposure probabilities, $\mathrm E[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm C}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]]\ge\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $\hat{\overline y}(d)$: supplement Equation (1), p. 1 (S8). $\pi_{ij}(d)=\Pr[D_i=D_j=d]$: supplement p. 3 (S8); the pairs $i=j$ are included in the double sums and have $\pi_{ii}(d)=\pi_i(d)>0$. $\overline y_i(d)$: Equation (5) of the main text, p. 6 (S5). $\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]$ under NURVA: supplement Equation (5), p. 3 (P061-T18). Condition 5.1: p. 8 (S7), read as in (S10)(d). $Y_i=y_i(\mathbf Z)$ (S3). ‘Conservative’ means the inequality (8) between the expectation of the estimator and the true variance.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P061-H6, the variance estimators; both readers derived these results and confirmed them by exact enumeration, including cases with zero joint probabilities (Opus: 220 cases, 110 with some zero joint exposure probability; Sol: three designs with signed outcomes and the ordered-pair multiplicities checked). Conservativeness is in expectation. The exact slack, derived when this list was fixed from Equation (5) and Equation (7) under NURVA and not printed in the paper, is $$\mathrm E[\widehat{\mathrm{Var}}_{\mathrm C}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]]-\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]=N^{-2}\sum_{(i,j):\pi_{ij}(d)=0}\tfrac12\big(\overline y_i(d)+\overline y_j(d)\big)^2\ge0,$$ since for an ordered pair with $\pi_{ij}(d)=0$ the term of Equation (5) is $-\overline y_i(d)\overline y_j(d)$ and the expectation of the corresponding term of Equation (7) is $\tfrac12\overline y_i(d)^2+\tfrac12\overline y_j(d)^2$; it may help a formalizer and is not itself a target. The supplement states that without NURVA such estimators ‘need not be unbiased or conservative’ (the Opus reader's example has expectation 2.90 against a variance of 6.05); that caveat is not part of this target. No error-class finding touches it.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplementary Appendix, ‘Unbiased covariate adjustment (without NURVA)’, Equation (10)
canonical_claim.location: Supplementary Appendix p. 7 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 7); announced in the main text on p. 14 (PDF p. 14)
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. Main text p. 14: ‘In a result we believe to be novel, we also show that finite-sample unbiasedness can be attained for covariate-adjusted estimators even if NURVA does not hold.’ Supplement p. 7: ‘Suppose we had (nonrandom) auxiliary information $\mathbf X_i\in\mathbb R^\ell$ for each unit $i$ and a set of candidate prediction functions $f_d:\mathbb R^\ell\times\mathcal B\to\mathbb R$ indexed by parameter vector $\beta$. Consider the following regression-type estimator: $$\hat{\overline y}_R(d)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{(Y_i-f_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta))\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}+\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Nf_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta).$$’ ‘Unbiased covariate adjustment (without NURVA). Suppose $\pi_i(d)>0$ and $$\mathrm E\Big[\frac{f_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta)\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}\Big]=\mathrm E[f_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta)],\quad\forall i.$$ This condition is satisfied, for example, when the prediction for unit $i$ is independent, or mean independent, of $\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}$. Then, $$\begin{aligned}\mathrm E[\hat{\overline y}_R(d)]&=\mathrm E\Big[\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{(Y_i-f_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta))\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}+\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Nf_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta)\Big]\\&=\mathrm E\Big[\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{Y_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{f_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta)\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}}{\pi_i(d)}+\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^Nf_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta)\Big]\\&=\overline y(d)-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[f_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta)]+\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathrm E[f_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta)]\\&=\overline y(d).\end{aligned}\qquad(10)$$’
Formal content. In the setting of Section 3, with no SUTVA or NURVA assumption: let $\pi_i(d)>0$ for every $i$ and let $F_i=f_d(\mathbf X_i,\hat\beta)$, $i=1,\ldots,N$, be real random variables (functions of the design vector $\mathbf Z$) with $\mathrm E[F_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}/\pi_i(d)]=\mathrm E[F_i]$ for every $i$. Then $\mathrm E[\hat{\overline y}_R(d)]=\overline y(d)$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $Y_i=y_i(\mathbf Z)$ (S3); $D_i$, $\pi_i(d)$: Equations (2) and (4) (S4, S5); $\overline y(d)$: Equation (6), p. 7 (S6); unbiasedness of the unadjusted estimator: supplement Equation (3) (P061-T16). $\mathbf X_i$ is nonrandom; $\hat\beta$ is the estimated parameter, a function of the observed data and hence random under the design; the supplement does not give $\hat\beta$ a unit index, while its prose speaks of ‘the prediction used for unit $i$’ (p. 7: “adjustment is unbiased when the prediction used for unit $i$ is constructed in a design-valid way, for example from auxiliary data or suitable cross-fitting”). The formal content therefore takes one prediction $F_i$ per unit, an arbitrary function of $\mathbf Z$ satisfying the displayed moment condition, which covers a common $\hat\beta$ and unit-specific (cross-fitted) $\hat\beta_i$ alike. Expectations are over the design distribution and are assumed to exist (automatic for a finite support).
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P061-H7; both readers followed the cancellation of the two prediction terms and verified it by exact enumeration with predictions that do not depend on the realized assignment, under interference. The result is conditional on the displayed moment condition, which is exactly what the proof uses; candidate P061-N013 (that a naive leave-one-out prediction from observed outcomes need not satisfy the condition under interference) was not confirmed as an error, since the text does not claim that it does. Whether the result is novel is not a mathematical statement and is not part of this target. For designs with infinite support the proof needs in addition the first-moment condition of P061-T8 and finite expectations of the predictions (finding P061-CAND-001, Minor); on a finite support the printed statement holds as it stands. The step from the second to the third line uses supplement Equation (3) for the first sum and the moment condition for the second.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Supplementary Appendix, Proposition 1 (consistency of the Horvitz–Thompson estimator under NURVA and Conditions 1.1–1.3)
canonical_claim.location: Supplementary Appendix p. 5 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 5); the proof sketch is on p. 6 (publisher-supplement.pdf p. 6)
canonical_claim.statement: As printed (supplement p. 5): ‘Condition 1.1. (Bounded reweighted revealable potential outcomes) $\Pr\Big[\Big|\frac{y_i(\mathbf Z)}{\pi_i(d)}\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}\Big|>c_{(N)}\Big]=0$ for a sequence $c_{(N)}$ and all $i,N$. Condition 1.2. (Restricted exposure dependence structure) $$\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N|\pi_{ij}(d)-\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)|=b_{(N)},$$ where $b_{(N)}=o(N^2)$. Condition 1.3. (Interaction condition) $b_{(N)}c_{(N)}^2=o(N^2)$. Proposition 1. With restrictions on variation in reweighted revealable potential outcomes, exposure dependence among units, and their interaction, (Conditions 1.1, 1.2, 1.3), as well as NURVA (Condition 5.1), the Horvitz-Thompson estimator $\hat{\overline y}(d)$ is consistent for the AEPO, $\overline y(d)$. Specifically, $$\hat{\overline y}(d)-\overline y(d)=o_p(1).$$’ Supplement p. 6: ‘The proof follows from plugging terms into the variance formula, and demonstrating that under the specified conditions, the estimation error converges to zero, using the unbiasedness result and the Chebyshev inequality.’
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The asymptotic regime: supplement p. 5 (S9): a sequence of finite populations $U_{(N)}$ indexed by the population size $N$, each with its own design $\mathbf Z_{(N)}$, feasible set $\mathcal Z_{(N)}$, exposure mappings $g_{i,(N)}$ and raw potential outcomes; “Assume that the range of $g_{i,(N)}|\mathrm{Supp}(\mathbf Z_{(N)})$ contains $d$, for all $i,N$” (so $\pi_i(d)>0$ in every population); the index $(N)$ on $y_i$, $\pi_i(d)$, $\pi_{ij}(d)$, $\hat{\overline y}(d)$ and $\overline y(d)$ is left implicit (note 2, p. 10). $\hat{\overline y}(d)$: supplement Equation (1), p. 1 (S8). $\overline y(d)$: Equation (6) of the main text, p. 7 (S6). $\pi_{ij}(d)=\Pr[D_i=D_j=d]$: supplement p. 3. Condition 5.1 (NURVA): main text p. 8 (S7), read as in (S10)(d), in every population of the sequence. $c_{(N)}$ and $b_{(N)}$ are sequences of nonnegative reals; $b_{(N)}$ is defined by the equality of Condition 1.2. $o(N^2)$: the ratio to $N^2$ tends to 0 as $N\to\infty$. $\hat{\overline y}(d)-\overline y(d)=o_p(1)$: for every $\epsilon>0$, $\Pr\big[|\hat{\overline y}(d)-\overline y(d)|>\epsilon\big]\to0$ as $N\to\infty$, the probability being under the design of the $N$th population.
canonical_claim.finite_lemmas: For each fixed $N$ (the steps the proof sketch names, written out in the validator's derivation for P061-N010, validate/_batch/P061-B02/work/derivations.md, and by both readers): (F1) unbiasedness, supplement Equation (3), p. 2: $\mathrm E[\hat{\overline y}(d)]=\overline y(d)$ (P061-T16). (F2) Under NURVA, supplement Equation (4), p. 2: $Y_i\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}=\overline y_i(d)\mathbb 1\{D_i=d\}$. (F3) The variance formula, supplement Equation (5), p. 3 (P061-T18). (F4) Under NURVA and Condition 1.1, $|\overline y_i(d)|/\pi_i(d)\le c_{(N)}$ for every $i$ (otherwise the event excluded by Condition 1.1 would have probability at least $\pi_i(d)>0$). (F5) Hence $\mathrm{Var}[\hat{\overline y}(d)]\le N^{-2}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N|\pi_{ij}(d)-\pi_i(d)\pi_j(d)|\,c_{(N)}^2=b_{(N)}c_{(N)}^2/N^2$. (F6) Chebyshev's inequality: for every $\epsilon>0$, $\Pr\big[|\hat{\overline y}(d)-\overline y(d)|>\epsilon\big]\le\dfrac{b_{(N)}c_{(N)}^2}{N^2\epsilon^2}$, which tends to 0 under Condition 1.3.
canonical_claim.note: Headline claim P061-H6, consistency; both readers proved the proposition from Conditions 1.1 and 1.3, NURVA and Chebyshev's inequality. It is the paper's only numbered proposition and its only asymptotic result with stated hypotheses. Two remarks from the validation of the neighbouring clarity note P061-N010, neither an error: the sentence before Condition 1.1 (‘what we require jointly from our regularity conditions is that the variance bound is $o(N^2)$’) names the unnormalized bound $b_{(N)}c_{(N)}^2$, while the variance of the mean estimator is bounded by $b_{(N)}c_{(N)}^2/N^2=o(1)$; and the separate restriction $b_{(N)}=o(N^2)$ of Condition 1.2 is not used in the proof once Condition 1.3 holds. The Lean statement should keep all three conditions as hypotheses, as printed, and not weaken the conclusion; (F1)–(F6) are exact for each $N$ and carry the whole argument, the limit being the last step of (F6). The claims about central limit theorems that follow the proposition on supplement p. 6 are attributions to other works and are not targets (see P061-T10).
